utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. First of all, very unfortunate where I was unable to sit yesterday; today it is Judge Fluegge who for urgent personal reasons is unable to sit with us. Judge Moloto and myself have considered whether it would be in the interests of justice to continue to hear the case and we concluded that it was. The Chamber was informed, Mr. Lukic, that the Defence wished to raise a preliminary matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. We are -- the Defence is facing difficulties with bringing the witnesses for the last working week in this month, since two of our witnesses cannot come and testify in that period of time. So we talked to the Prosecution and we think that we found a solution, but we proposed some new witnesses in our motion from the 24th of March, 2015, and one of them is willing and able to attend the proceedings in that week, and it is Simic, Savo. So we kindly ask Your Honours to decide on our motion as soon as possible so we can continue with the preparations and bringing of this witness to testify in front of Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If only for that witness to say the least.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At least for that witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider that. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we have spoken, and Mr. Weber has -- can handle that. We would appreciate any more information or statements regarding the person as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that we spoke with Mr. Weber. There is a statement from Karadzic trial for this witness and we will be using that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. The Chamber is now aware of the urgency of deciding and -- certainly in respect of that witness. We'll give it priority. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe this helps the Chamber expedite things. The Prosecution has no objection to the adding of the witness and actually what we need -- we understand he's going to be testifying based on his past statement. So if we could get the 92 ter motion sooner rather than later, that would be optimal for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the 92 ter motion, but the first issue is adding him to the witness list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the -- if there are no other preliminaries, then could the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, before we continue I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, and Mr. McCloskey will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This morning we'll get into a bit more of the -- your testimony yesterday about the documents and a bit about communication. So if we could start off with Exhibit 2 -- P2109, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think you are recorded as you pronounced. Does it start with a 2 before the P, that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you'll recall - and we can see - this is the 11 July 1995 document that you testified was typewritten which we agree with you on that point. And it is -- if we can go to the next page in the English and the original document, we can see that this order is under the name of the commander, Colonel-General Ratko Mladic. And it has s.r. handwritten in the original next to Mladic's name. And you talked about that a bit as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So could we go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you also, I recall, yesterday talked about another document that was sent from the comms branch and it had a particular strictly confidential number. Do you remember what that strictly confidential number started out with from the comms -- your comms branch in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was 04-12, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, that's what you testified yesterday to. Now, looking at this document, we see it's strictly confidential number 03/4. Now, that's from Miletic's operations sector, is it not, that number for 1995?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if we look at the context of this order, we see that it's, would you agree with me, a rather serious situation that Mladic is describing. We see in the second paragraph he says that there is verified information that the command of the 28th Division, Srebrenica, has asked the command of the so-called Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and basically it says for forces to come from the Sarajevo theatre over to the Srebrenica theatre. And we can see that the order is to take the following measures and that it's a very urgent order. And the Court understands the context of what was going on on 11 July in Srebrenica and so I think we can all understand this context. The Court has also heard evidence that General Mladic was in the Srebrenica area for most of the day on the 11th of July; is that your knowledge as well?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My knowledge was not of that nature. I didn't know where General Mladic was. There was no need for me to know that either, but putting that aside I really didn't know where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if General Mladic is made aware that in the theatre where he is leading combat actions, that serious reinforcements are coming from the enemy, and when he receives that kind of information would he not be able to communicate to his Main Staff to get an order out to the appropriate units to take care of that situation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the command post of the Main Staff, there were officers who could look into that and take measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please answer the question, Witness. The question was whether Mr. Mladic -- whether he would be able to communicate with his Main Staff to get an order out under those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Mladic couldn't get on the comms system that we know had an RRU-1 at Pribicevac, the forward command post of the Srebrenica operation, or perhaps a radio-relay system set up at the Bratunac Brigade and speak to the Main Staff, speak to Miletic or one of his operations people and say: Get this order out, we have information the Muslims are being reinforced. Couldn't he have done that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if he had been able to get to a telephone line to call the Main Staff, he couldn't send this kind of message. If he had gotten in contact with the officers in the Main Staff, the only thing that he could do was to take all the necessary measures. And then those officers would know what measures should be taken and that's what they wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not suggesting General Mladic is encrypting or typing the document himself. All I'm saying is that he calls his operations people, informs them of this dire situation, and tells them to get out an order to make sure that this situation is dealt with. He could certainly do that, couldn't he?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he could have done something of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it would be also true, would it not be, if the operations branch or someone else, the security and intel branch at the Main Staff received this kind of information, they could have been in contact with Mladic, either through the Pribicevac forward command post or the Bratunac Brigade, and informed him of that information and received his orders regarding how to deal with it. That could have been done as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The centre at Pribicevac, General Mladic certainly didn't use that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you say you didn't even know where he was, so let's answer my question. It was just the reverse of the first. If the Main Staff operations people or security and intel people contacted Mladic regarding this information, he would have been able to inform them to get an order out from the Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sending the order differs from conveying a message that measures should be taken. Sending an order means that an order has to be typed and dispatched. There is a difference there. That's my answer. He could not send an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to get back to what seems to be the origin of the question. You already testified that General Mladic could contact the Main Staff if he wanted to exchange views or whatever. Then the question was whether the Main Staff could contact Mr. Mladic in urgent situations so that they could exchange views or have a conversation. Was that possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that they engaged in such a conversation because communication with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I didn't ask you whether they did. I just asked you whether the communications were such that the Main Staff could contact Mr. Mladic or Mr. Mladic could contact -- and Mr. Mladic could contact the Main Staff in order to briefly discuss whatever was there to be discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They couldn't contact when they were on the move.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, already in one of the previous answers you contacted that at least Mr. Mladic could tell the Main Staff about measures that they would have to take under such urgent circumstances. So at least part of your present answer is contradicting your previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask for the B/C/S to be re-translated because in the B/C/S he gave a different answer than was interpreted in English as a -- one option. The B/C/S had two options.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Which one, Mr. Ivetic, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My understanding was when they were stationary, they could; when they were in movement, they could not. That was the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was, as a matter of fact, trying to find out which page, which line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But could -- yes. I asked you whether communication was such that the Main Staff could contact Mr. Mladic or Mr. Mladic could contact the Main Staff, or rather, and Mr. Mladic could contact the Main Staff in order to briefly discuss whatever was there to be discussed. Could you please repeat the answer you gave to that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that communication was possible when General Mladic was in a situation to get to the centre. I don't know whether he did. When in movement, he could not communicate. Communication was not possible in movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- let me just wait for a second. Speaking at an inaudible level, please. Mr. McCloskey, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If -- yesterday you testified that in the Puch vehicle, the military vehicle, Mladic had communications; right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if he's in and around that vehicle, he can communicate to the Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The radio telephone in General Mladic's vehicle was not functioning, so he would use it rarely or not at all, and I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Witness, yesterday you said in civilian vehicles that were used by General Mladic, there was communications equipment that he could use. Now, if equipment is not functional, you can't use it, isn't it? That --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Not civilian --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, he said there's nothing in civilian but he did have it in his Puch vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just read it again. Yes, I see that. It's a terrain vehicle and that's a vehicle that usually commanders had. And it was about devices that were installed on those vehicles. Radio telephone devices -- you didn't say yesterday that it wasn't functioning in any way, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is done by radio-repeater devices. There has to be a repeater in one of the elevations for them to function, but the repeaters did not function. Their range was such that he really could not use his communication device in the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Depending on where he was or in general?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In general. Our repeaters were not functioning. There were no spare parts so they became obsolete and unusable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday you said, when asked: These radio telephone devices, based on what technology did they operate, what type were they? Electromagnetic waves, you said, but the range was short and it depended on repeaters --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- only, their range depended on that, that is -- and then you said that this was installed on the Puch. Yesterday you didn't say it wasn't functioning at all because repeaters were not functioning. You were saying that it depended on the range of the repeaters. Is that what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that radio telephone device communication was conditional upon radio repeaters on the elevations, in the territory controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska. At first we did mount them; however, that system very soon became unusable because of the lack of spare parts. We could not maintain those repeaters for a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why didn't you say this yesterday? Why didn't you say yesterday it was a useless system because no spare parts, it didn't function at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't asked that. I was only asked what system of communications we used, and I gave you an example of just one such system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you gave us -- well, I leave it to that. Mr. McCloskey, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The Court has seen video of Mr. Mladic driving in his Puch vehicle approaching Srebrenica between Zeleni Jadar and Srebrenica. And they've also heard evidence that the Drina Corps had a communications van fully set up with an RRU-1 in Pribicevac on a hill above this area within a few kilometres. So certainly anybody with a good radio, as you've described, in a Puch can communicate directly to the Drina Corps comms van up on the hill above them in Pribicevac a few kilometres away; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was able to get to Pribicevac, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Pribicevac could speak to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could speak to the Main Staff via the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me get back to where I originally was trying to get to. So if General Mladic, having received this vital intel information about potential Muslim reinforcements to his area and he decided to issue an order, the order that we see - I think it's still on the screen - the unsigned order would come in this format, would it not, if Mladic issued the order to the operations people they could have typed it up, put in the details, and sent it off, just like this one?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic could not issue an order to his operatives in this form. This document prepared to be transmitted by telegram could have been drafted in only one place and that was in the operative staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. General Mladic could only say: Take all measures, if he had gotten in contact with them, and I don't know whether he did, I was not there, I was not with him. He could have only said: Take measures to prevent surprises or something like that. And for him to draft such a document and to then send it, no, he didn't -- he couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be no disagreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we don't disagree, sir. I'm not suggesting he's drafting it or sending it but --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Actually, when counsel used this document with another witness, he did, he indicated that s.r. meant that General Mladic had personally signed the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's not what we're talking about, whether he signed it or not. We're not even there yet. Nice signal to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Butler, the Prosecution expert, that this document was used and that was said by this same attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, that's not to be conveyed to the witness under those circumstances. You can be critical about it, you can argue about it, but it's not information that should be sent to the witness at this moment. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And yesterday, on page temporary 35223, line 23, you were asked by Mr. Ivetic in regard to this document: "What are the obligations of an encryptions officer receiving an original that is unsigned? What can they do?" And your answer was: "He has to transmit it because it was brought to him by somebody who has the authority to send telegrams." So, in your view, this, what you're calling an original typed order, was sent?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not retyped. It was typed. The order was not retyped. It was typed. It's the original order and it was dispatched.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it had to be dispatched because the encryptor received it from someone with the authority to send telegrams and in this case -- was that correct as you stated?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in this case, it would likely have been someone from the operations branch, since this came from the operations branch as we know from the number?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the operations branch would not have put Mladic's name at the bottom of this unless they had the authority from Mladic to do so; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you've testified at 35223 that s.r. doesn't mean anything.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in this case it didn't mean anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's right. And in other cases, what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In other cases, if it was really signed personally by General Mladic, a document, then the encryptor is obliged to put s.r. there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that in Serbian means"svojerucno"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in his own hand, "svojerucni potpis [phoen]": Signature in his own hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: S.r. abbreviated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now let's go to that second page of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it wouldn't surprise you that Svetozar Andric just testified in this case that "svojerucno," "s.r," meant that -- it meant someone had signed a document in their own hand or it had been signed by the person; basically what you just said?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, you are asked to repeat what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor said that Svetozar Andric said that "svojerucno" means that he signed it and would that surprise me, and I said no that would not surprise me that that's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that was on transcript 34887, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this rather -- you'll agree with me, this rather serious document that we see is stamped, somebody has written in s.r. so a -- on this document. That should have been written by someone from the operations branch; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most probably that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And given the seriousness of the -- General Miletic and his operations branch at time of war, someone wrote this down for a particular reason, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably so, judging by the seriousness of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when one sees "s.r," that is meant to convey that the person whose name is on the document was aware of it, correct, at the very least?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily, not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I think we've made our point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I noticed that the stamp which appears immediately next to or even over the name of Mr. Mladic is not mentioned in the translation, the stamp of the command. The other stamp is mentioned but this one is not and also not the text of that stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and we noted yesterday that there was actually a typo in the date on the English translation which is, as you can see in that bottom stamp, 13 July. So we'll get you a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But could you then include this -- the lack of reference to that round stamp as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's right and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the extent possible, also if the parties could agree on the text of that stamp, that would be appreciated as well. I see it starts with General Staff, at least from what I understand from the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in that regard, let's go to Exhibit 65 ter 25760.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, what we're going to see, and I've discussed this with Mr. Ivetic to inform him, is an almost -- no, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is this 25760?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Switch off your mike, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, could we have the same number but c.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, this is an identical version of the typewritten order that you've seen, sir, but the one you saw was a scanned copy of -- from the barracks that we received this. This particular document is the -- what we picked up at the actual barracks, and I want to show this just to hand it to you because we've been talking about originals, and I just want to show you this which is as original as we get and ask you whether it is truly an original or what. So if we could get some help from the usher, we could hand this document to the person. The Bench can see it. It's -- as well and I mentioned this to Mr. Ivetic. And for everyone, there's a bright blue stamp on the back page of it and that is the stamp that was given to us recently when we retrieved it from the barracks, so that doesn't have anything to do with the war-time nature of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're now looking at the -- could we have a look at the English translation as well, especially the handwriting, or is it the same -- or is there no English translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see a translation of some handwriting which apparently does not correspond with either of the originals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This will be -- the problem will be revealed soon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, you're looking on the back. And, just so you know, that is the stamp that we got recently from the Serb authorities, within the last few years when they gave that to us, so that shouldn't be viewed as part of the original document.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this one was drafted later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're referring to the stamp on the very back of the document?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So looking at this, what we both agreed is a typewritten document, this isn't original and, for example, it's not original type ink, it's not original -- I mean it's not type ink, you don't see stamp ink on the front. This more looks like a photocopy, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a photocopied document. And I have to say we're talking about the 13th of July. This act bears the date the 15th of July, not the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you please limit yourself to answer the questions. There's no need for spontaneous comments. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, it's the 15th. So was there a -- did your comms place where the encryption machine was or in the nearby vicinity was there a photocopy machine?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have a photocopy machine in the unit for encryption or encoding and decoding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did the operations sector have a photocopy machine?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So it's possible the operations branch photocopied this and brought it to you or would they have only brought you an original, stamped document to encrypt?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would always be the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think there's a need to enter that into evidence. It may just confuse the issue so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it in your hands. And if the Prosecution -- if the Defence takes a different position, we'll hear from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I think the record is clear as to what the witness has talked about and I think it's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If we could get it back, thanks. Now let's go to Exhibit 65 ter 25760b.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, we can see that this is the same date, title, strictly confidential number, and this is a Teletype or a telegram, an encrypted telegram version of what we've been seeing, is it not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please enlarge the document a bit. I don't see it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could the -- if the usher could help, and I would be handing him a copy of the typewritten document and a copy of the Teletype document so he can compare them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I've already seen these, so there's no need to show me. You can give them directly to the witness, no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, sir, just take a look and you'll notice there's been some highlighting on both those documents which I'll ask you about in a minute, but can you confirm that the -- what we're seeing was the typewritten document and then the -- a copy of the encrypted document. In this case, this was sent to one of the addresses, the -- I think the 1st Podrinje Brigade, the Rogatica Brigade, as we can see from the signature of Gojkovic on the top. So do these look -- is that correct? Sorry -- to simplify the question. This is the Teletyped version of the typed version?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that -- yes, correct, but the square stamp is missing on the telegram of the received -- the party that received it, so the telegram is not complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So for the Rogatica Brigade to have followed the book completely, they would have had to put another stamp on it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It has not been properly received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we looked this over carefully last night and would you agree that the document -- or the same document aside from the little marked areas in red which we thought were just a matter of slight typing mistakes by the encryptor, from our view. So could you compare the little marks highlighted in red to see if you think that there are significant differences that may suggest it was encrypted from a different document or that these are just little mistakes that the encryptor made as he typed the document into the machine, if you can tell.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two reasons for the errors. One of them is that the person who processed it mistyped it; and the second one is that there were interruptions on the line and that some things were inserted that was sent by the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. But you would conclude that this encrypted document reflects the typed document?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer the Teletype version.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objections, but we've been talking about markings --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... 60b into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We've been talking about marked ones. Do you want the marked one in or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, I don't think -- the only marked ones were for his opinion regarding whether they were one and the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, you referred to red markings. This Chamber doesn't know what markings are in red so it would like to see it anyhow --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then perhaps for the completeness of the record, it might be better to have it in as well so that at least what is red and what's not red is clear to everyone who would look into this matter later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not sure red will show up so I can give a version where the red marks are circled and get those into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you could agree on that with Mr. Ivetic, that would be appreciated, and meanwhile the Chamber would like to have a look at the original as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, if we can pass that. And, Your Honours, for your knowledge, the translation that had the problems in it was a translation of the Teletype version, and there were several Teletype versions. As you could see, there were several addressees. So the translation was -- for the typewritten was fundamentally the same but, as you pointed out, a few small differences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it may not even be necessary to have the red markings into -- in evidence because they were just -- it's highlighting by a marker which is on three spots. The first on the first page, directly under B, where the typewritten version is quite -- is slightly different from the word "supivjanska" as it appears in the original. The same under the heading under "naredjujem 1A" the word "zatvaraju" is slightly different in the encoded version. And the third appears under the word in a paragraph which is starting with K3 where the word "voda" in the encoded version seems to be "vodova" in the typewritten version. That's all the differences. There's no need to have it in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Except, Your Honours, I think that the telegram version has been tendered. I think that also should be in evidence. We haven't yet given that a number, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 25760b will be MFI P7372, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7372 is marked for identification. Please proceed. We have two or three minutes left to the break, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm very close to being finished. If I could just rearrange myself, I think I will be able to finish up pretty soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Pretty soon" is a vague notion. Before the break or after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we break now, I think I can finish up in 15 or 20 minutes, depending on how crazy it gets, but just a couple questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How it develops, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How it develops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will take the break first. Witness, we would like to see you back in 20 minutes. We will take a break now and it will not take long after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, we'll now continue with your cross-examination. Mr. McCloskey, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, just a -- hopefully a few questions about your work at the -- and knowledge at the Main Staff about radio-relay communications. Now, I believe you said that you -- in March of 1995 you left the regiment and moved to a different job. And when you said you left the regiment or the comms regiment, was that the 67th Communications Regiment?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that was located in Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you left that position and took a position where precisely?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communications department, the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. Desk officer for cryptographic data protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that was under Prole and was also in Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time that was the case. And then Colonel Prole got ill and his deputy, Lieutenant-Colonel Mirsad Radakovic, was in Krajina at the forward command post too. So I was on my own in the communications department. Along the line of command and control, the chief of communications was replaced by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last name. At that time the commander of communications regiment, Colonel Nedeljko Gredo, stood in for the chief of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you would have known a Velo Pajic at that time, would you not have?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Velo Pajic was the commander of the telephone platoon in the company for communications for three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And would that have been in the -- of the 67th Communications Regiment?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 67th Communications Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you were both in the 67th Communications Regiment at the same time?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a company commander and Velo Pajic worked at Goljak-1 feature where he was engaged on establishing and maintaining telephone lines. He was the commander of a platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was his rank in 1995?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you have a son that was in communications with the 65th Protection Regiment in Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you have a son that was in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had two sons in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was they in 1995?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One was at Goljak-1 facility where he was an encoder in 1995 and the other was affiliated with the police station in Zvornik, where he worked as a communications guy, or rather, a signals man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, when Mr. Ivetic was talking to you, you spoke a bit about the encrypted lines between Veliki Zep, which the Trial Chamber's heard quite a bit about. And you concluded that the lines from Veliki Zep to the various brigades were all encrypted. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something similar, but I have to correct you just a little. I said that the lines from the Main Staff, i.e., from Veliki Zep, to subordinated units, and those were corps commands, the Presidency, and the air force and anti-aircraft defence in Banja Luka and Zarozine [phoen] were encrypted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and in fact on page 35207 when Mr. Ivetic asked you: First of all, which routes could be encrypted? You answered: "Could have and had to have been encrypted ..." And then you named all the corps, including the Drina Corps. Now, wasn't there a route between Veliki Zep and the Drina Corps that was not encrypted?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a radio-relay route from Veliki Zep to the Drina Corps which used an RRU-800 device and that was not encrypted. But that was mostly used by the Drina Corps, and the Main Staff used only one part of the channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you would like to correct your testimony of yesterday that they had to have been encrypted and that they were encrypted because there was -- there was one route that wasn't encrypted?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe we spoke at cross-purposes. I'm talking about RRU-800. I said that there was an encrypted route. Now, as to whether there were other radio-relay routes between the corps command and the Main Staff, if there was, I would have said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the witness is speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the last part of his answer. You were speaking too fast, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Ivetic asked me if there were encrypted routes and I said that there were. If he had asked me if there were any other routes, I'm sure that I would have answered, yes, there was a radio relay route leading to the Drina Corps using an RRU-800 device which was not encrypted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I won't dwell on this, but you -- when he asked you if -- which routes could be encrypted, you said: "Could have and had to have been encrypted ..." And then you listed the Drina Corps as one of those. You've specifically failed to mention that there was a route that was -- didn't have to be encrypted and wasn't encrypted. Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand, but he did not ask me how many radio-relay routes were towards the Drina Corps. I said that there was an encrypted route. I didn't say that there was a non-encrypted route. If he had asked me if there was another one, I'm sure that I would have mentioned a radio-relay route that was not encrypted and that used the RRU-800 radio-relay device.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So do you know about the routes from the Drina Corps to the brigades, were those encrypted?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radio-relay routes from the Drina Corps to the to the brigades were not encrypted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Ivetic, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just a few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could start off from here where we just ended with the Prosecution's cross. With regard to the radio-relay route between Veliki Zep and the Drina Corps, which radio-relay device was used by the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two types: One FM-200 which was encrypted on a special route; and another RRU-800 which was not encrypted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And of these two, was there any difference in the frequency of use?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A huge difference. The information that contained a degree confidentiality were sent along encrypted lines. Encoded telegrams were sent via the RRU-800 device because they were already encrypted and thus protected at the source. Therefore, there was no need to use the encrypted route to send coded, or rather, already-encrypted telegrams.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to P2180, you were shown a highlighted version that had some typographical differences. And at temporary transcript page 20, you said that the differences could result from the person who processed it mistyping it or interruptions in the line. Could you please explain for us that part of your answer dealing with interruptions in the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for my clarification, Mr. Lukic -- Mr. Ivetic, P2180, I don't seem to remember it being shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, I apologise. It was P7372 that was shown to the witness that was highlighted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer. A coder may make a mistake, a typing mistake, but it is also possible that along the route due to weather conditions and disturbances that reflect on teleprinter communications. As a result, there is a surplus of symbols or signs or a shortfall of signs on the final version, hence the mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at temporary transcript page 15, you said the initials s.r. on a telegram did not necessarily denote that the person whose name appears on the same is aware of the same. Could you explain your answer?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: S.r. doesn't mean that the person indicated actually signed the telegram, and this is a very obvious example because this telegram was never signed by General Ratko Mladic -- actually, nobody signed it, although it does say s.r., which means in one's own hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now at temporary transcript page 13, you were asked if the operations branch of the Main Staff would not put General Mladic's name unless they had authority to do so and you said that was correct. The question I have for you is as follows: Did the operations branch have to seek authority from General Mladic every time they wanted to send a telegram in his name?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Along the line of command and control, the commander of the Main Staff should --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he did not have to request -- so the operative staff did not have to ask General Mladic's permission to send a telegram of this kind. In the first possible scenario, the operative staff was duty-bound to inform their commander about the activities that were carried out in his absence, including the telegrams that were sent, and also the purpose of those telegrams.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can inquire with the interpreters, do they think we got the whole answer or should I ask him to repeat the answer based upon --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't get the whole answer. We missed the first half of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you guide the witness, because you know what may be missing, what needs to be supplemented. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I can ask you to repeat your answer. The last -- the part that got lost, according to the transcript, is as follows: We heard you say: Along the line of command and control, the commander of the Main Staff should ... and then there we lost the middle part of your answer. Could you please repeat what you said from that point forward.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS is absent, he is replaced by the Chief of Staff of the VRS. In this case, the Chief of Staff was also absent. If the Chief of Staff is absent, then it would be the operative centre that would take over all those duties. The operative centre was headed by the chief of the operative centre. The operative centre did not have to request approval from General Mladic for drafting and sending all of the orders that concerned the life and work of the Army of Republika Srpska. Having said that, the operative centre was duty-bound to inform the commander at first opportunity about the activities that they had carried out and the telegrams that had been sent in his absence, as well as the purpose of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, those are all the questions that I have for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Witness, I would have the following question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you think that anyone would dare to send out an order with the name of General Mladic under it if that person was not convinced that General Mladic would have given the instructions for such an order?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You think that no one would dare to do that unless, is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they would dare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's your position that people would send out an order with General Mladic's name under it even if they were not convinced that this was in line with what General Mladic wanted to be ordered?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have an explanation as to why subordinates would send an order, as you say, would dare to send an order not being convinced that it would be in line with the position taken by your superior?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have an explanation, but I assume that that person at the moment when he was drafting that order thought that that was the best solution, given the moment and circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Told by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't see the word "told" in the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, no you're right, Mr. Ivetic. I may have misheard. But would they then not issue that order under their own name rather than to make it an order by a superior of which they were not convinced yet or not convinced that that superior would support that order?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it sounds and looks differently, when you receive an order that was supposed to have been signed by General Ratko Mladic as opposed to somebody else. Everybody obeyed and respected General Mladic. His orders were carried out, no questions asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would abuse his name in order to enforce that the subordinates would follow that order, though it didn't come from General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: God forbid, I wouldn't. But I suppose that there were such cases as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On what is that supposition based? Could you give us an example?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we go back to the telegram that was the topic of our conversation here, you can see that that telegram was not drafted by General Mladic, although his name is indicated on it and somebody also made an indication of his signature in his own hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you're moving away from what I asked you. It was not about sending a document, but it was by sending an order which the person who sent it or at least the person who took responsibility for the drafting was not convinced that it was supported by General Mladic. That's the issue I raised with you. Such a way to abuse the name of General Mladic to give extra importance to an order, which he was unaware of.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm with you now completely. In the majority of those cases, the persons who put his name on an order thought that General Mladic would have supported that. But I also said that that was not across the board and that there may have been, or rather, that there were probably exceptions to that rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, apart from the specific case we addressed, do you have any other examples where someone was sending an order where it became clear that although General Mladic's name was used, that he did not support that or had not given instructions to send out this order? Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If Your Honour could be more precise. We talked about several telegrams yesterday in your absence; two in particular, I think, that we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm focusing on the one we looked at this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So could you give us an example, other than that one where General Mladic's name was abused by sending out an order under his name without his support?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any specific examples. I don't recall it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions triggered by -- Mr. McCloskey no. Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just a few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at P02125 in e-court. This is a document we looked at yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No speaking aloud, Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is dated the 15th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Looking at this document and recalling your testimony from yesterday, sir, that Mr. Mladic was not in the Main Staff on this day, does this refresh your recollection as to the question that the Judge just asked you about if you're aware of any other instances of documents conveying orders going out under General Mladic's name where you suspect that he had not signed it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, it's leading and it misrepresents my question. My question was not whether Mr. Mladic was present, but whether an order would be sent out abusing the name of General Mladic. And if he's not present, that doesn't necessarily mean that it abuses his name, abuse in the sense of that he did not support such an order to be issued. Therefore, please rephrase your question if you consider that it's still relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour, because you're missing in a part of your question that said: Or had not given instructions to send out this order. That's the second part of your question, so the fact that we had evidence yesterday is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you misunderstood the "or."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, if I did, then maybe perhaps the witness did too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then please, as I said, please rephrase your question. But I could ask the witness: This document which appears on the screen now, Mr. Stevanovic, do you have any information as this -- that this order was issued against the wishes or without knowledge or support of General Mladic, irrespective of where he was at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Specifically in this telegram General Mladic's name was not used, but actually it was done without his knowledge. He did not sign this document. He wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. But do you have any fact to your knowledge that General Mladic, his name was abused here, that is, that he did not wish this order to be sent out but that the person who did tried to give it additional importance by using the name of General Mladic without any knowledge of him supporting this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The proper thing would have been in this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, Witness, I stop you there --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I asked you whether you have any facts to your knowledge as I explained to you. What the way would have been that this order should have been issued is not my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this specific case, General Ratko Mladic's signature was not misused or his name was not misused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no -- Mr. Ivetic, you said you had a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just one follow-up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you do so, Mr. Ivetic. You raised a point that the question by Judge Orie said "or support." Now, I want to read to you page 33, lines 11 to 13, where the question was asked and if you can tell us whether the word "or" is there. "So could you give us an example other than that one where General Mladic's name was abused by sending out an order under his name without his support." There's no "or" there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The original question by the Judge before I asked for it to be more precise said that "or had not been given instructions to be sent out." Which is 33, lines 3 through 4, Your Honours, which still would have been in the witness's mind as the original question with just more details in the follow-up that is in the lines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm talking about the question that was -- that the witness specifically gave an answer to that you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is the question, Your Honours. That is the beginning of the question. I intervened to make it more precise, and then the part that you read was read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that is the question the witness answered?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Both of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Any further questions, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, just one or two in relation to this document that's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to -- I didn't in my questions -- if it's relevant in relation to my question, then of course please proceed. But I didn't bring up this document, so therefore the mere fact that it's on our screen is not sufficient. But if it relates to my question, then you may answer -- then you may put questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't know if we're having a miscommunication or not, but I've been saying now the third time that at temporary transcript page 34, line 25, through temporary transcript page 33, line 4, part of Your Honour's question indicated: Do you know any other examples where someone was sending an order where it became clear that although General Mladic's name was used that he did not support that or had not given instructions to send out this order." So it is -- my question is in this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you put this document to the witness, and after some quarrelling the witness said that this was not an instant of abuse. The question I did put to the witness, and it was clear, that it is about abuse, one way or another, not just not having given specific instructions if that is -- but again if it relates to my question - that's what I said, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is there a problem with the transcript, the part that I just read? Is that not the question that you asked that's recorded in the transcript, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may put a question to the witness and we'll then decide --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- or even Judge Moloto will decide whether it relates to that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Looking at the document that we have on our screen now, sir, and given your knowledge of the factual circumstances surrounding the same, did General Mladic have prior knowledge of this order before it was sent out?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, this is a Teletype, right, this isn't the original, or -- you called it the fact document that would have been handed to the encryptor?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a Teletype.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the original document, the fact document, could very well have been signed by General Mladic in his own hand, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been, but in this specific case it couldn't have been, he did not sign it because he wasn't at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You, a major in charge of encryptions, knows that General Mladic was not at the Main Staff at any time on the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't there on the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What gives you God's powers to know that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, could you please phrase your question in such a way without invoking any --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Understood, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- deity.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I would inquire is the Prosecution changing their position as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey will now first rephrase his question, and if there's any objection to that, Mr. Ivetic, we'll hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, the Court understands, has seen evidence about the villa at Crna Rijeka, the cabins at Crna Rijeka, the underground facility at Crna Rijeka. How is it, sir, that you, an encryptor, knows that Mladic wasn't there at any time on 15 July?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was physically present in the Crna Rijeka area on the 15th of July at Goljak-1 and Goljak, and I probably would have seen him. I didn't need to have any special powers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, then let's try to get matters clear. Are you telling us that he wasn't there or that you didn't see him and that you would have expected to see him if he was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He wasn't there. I didn't expect to see him. Had he been there, I would have probably known it. At the entrance of not the villa but the building where General Mladic would stay is where the Goljak-1 facility was. So I would have seen him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are talking about probabilities of seeing him and at the same time you say he wasn't there. But in the improbable case that he was there, that you didn't see him, is that still an option or is there any way you could exclude that option?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we didn't understand each other. I said probably. And what I meant was -- to say was that I would have seen him. But let me cut it short. He was not there on the 15th. He wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not fully understandable in light of your explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me clarify once again. Had General Mladic been there in the Crna Rijeka area, in Crna Rijeka itself, I would have seen him for sure since my post required me to walk from Goljak-1 to the cabins, and while I covered that route I would pass by the building used by General Mladic. Had he been there, I would have seen him. Had he been at the cabins, I would also have seen him. Because I didn't see him at either of those places or because I didn't run into him, and I knew from before that he was absent, all that points to the fact that he was not in the Crna Rijeka area on the 15th and he could not have signed this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Final question from me: Did you know -- do you know where he was during that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stevanovic, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench and travel home safely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One point still remaining, Your Honours. I'd still like to know from the Prosecution have they changed their position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness is excused. He is now putting his --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you may follow the usher. You are excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to know from the Prosecution if they're changing their position. As Your Honours perhaps might recall, there is a stipulation entered into by the Prosecution and the Defence that Mr. Mladic was not present in Crna Rijeka on the 15th but rather was in Belgrade. So this entire line of questioning at the end baffles me, given the stipulation that this Prosecution has entered into and that Your Honours are aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have to look exactly at what was stipulated. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I don't mind being questioned by Mr. Ivetic and to try to relieve his bafflement, but if I could have the agreement so that we can see it because I don't think he's got it right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. We'll have a look at it later. You review it, you'll check what Mr. Ivetic asked you. I think to clarify this matter if there would be a change - I'm not saying that there is - that it would be good for us to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think there has been, but we'll sort it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. The usher has left the courtroom. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honour, it's Mr. Janko Kecman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll wait for Mr. Kecman to be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, while we're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, could I already in anticipation of the questioning, ask that the title above paragraph 7 of his statement -- but I may have missed any -- I have some difficulties in understanding how this relates to anything in paragraph 7 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 7 from my information report or from the statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, from the statement. Yes, but we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Title -- [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- I draw your attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Above paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the relation between 7 to 11 and the title appearing above paragraph 7. Mr. Kecman, good morning. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Kecman. Mr. Kecman, you'll now first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You'll find Mr. Lukic to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would just kindly ask for the assistance of the usher so I hand this hard copy of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Kecman.

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you at any point provide a statement to the Defence of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. That was last year and the date is written here, it was the 28th of April, 2014.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to approach the microphone and speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you come closer to the microphone, please, and speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kecman, before we begin with the attestation, could we just look at page 3.

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we could have 1D1714 on our screens, please. So we need page 3 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why are we looking at page 3, Mr. Kecman? The reason for that is because Judge Orie asked why the title or the heading above paragraph 7 up to paragraph 11 states: Marking of apartments and burning of candles, but we don't see in the text what the heading refers to. So I just wanted to ask you if you could explain that to us. Do you have an explanation for it?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, when we talked -- I can just briefly tell you that I went through the whole area, the Republic of Slovenia, the Republic of Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, so these paragraphs from 7 to 11 talk about my status in the Republic of Croatia, that of my family, as well as in all the other areas where we worked in the period of 1991 to 1995. I'm talking about the Republic of Slovenia. I see there are a number of issues here so I could clarify each one, one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There's no need for that.

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will go back to that then, to the question of why this heading is above this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But could the witness then - unless you have any follow-up questions. What I do not understand is that the word "marking" doesn't appear anywhere, no marking of apartments, in paragraphs 7 to 11. And "burning of candles" also does not appear there. So I'm puzzled by the heading of these paragraphs. "Marking of apartments" and burning of candles." Do you have an explanation of how that relates to what I read in paragraphs 7 to 11?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's very simple. The settlement where I lived, it was a military neighbourhood in Zagreb, and I'm talking about other areas as well of the Republic of Croatia where the units of the JNA were located. The apartments of Serb and other people who did not belong to the Croat ethnic group in order to know exactly who was where - and I'm noting that this was after the first multi-party elections in Croatia - there was a great deal of dislike against members of the JNA. For example, in Slovenia, they experienced the JNA as an occupation army and they never agreed with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, let me stop you there. So I do understand that you could have made any factual observations about what happened at a certain period of time, at a certain place about marking of apartments and burning of candles, though you didn't do it in your statement. If that is what you're telling me, then it is at least clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted to emphasise once again. All members of the former -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not seeking that. I'm just establishing that what you could have said about marking of apartments and burning of candles in factual terms, that it is not there in paragraphs 7 to 11.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you permit me, I just wanted to look at the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Lukic, I take it that this same thought would have come to the mind of the person who added or made these titles. You're presenting the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can I try to further clarify but shortly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well clarify --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can work without the title -- without that title.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- Did you ask this title to be put there, Witness, "marking of apartments and burning of candles"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in my conversation and during the proofing, I stated the activities that happened in 1991 chronologically. One of those activities that I and my family and my colleagues experienced was that. And I can just give you one case that was the most striking example in 1991 -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I now understand that it has been subject during your conversations, that it appears in a title but that no factual information about such things happening appears in the statement. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will probably upload redacted version without this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, of course not. It's not -- I'm not a bureaucrat. I'm someone who tries to understand what is presented to him, and I now understand that the title is totally misplaced there, and I would have expected the Defence, who presents such a statement, to find that out if it takes me just three minutes to find that out. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kecman --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have the first page on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kecman, if you would, please, concentrate on the questions and answer the questions. On the first page, do you see the signature, do you recognise the signature on the document?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, Mr. Lukic, it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have the last page on the same document, please, in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And do you see the signature on the last page, Mr. Kecman, and do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, Mr. Lukic, that is also my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
