utterances.text: Other than the heading that we just looked at and that it does not comport with the rest of the statement, is the rest of the statement correctly recorded based on what you told the Defence of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I believe that everything that I had read is correct. Perhaps I would not be able to repeat it word by word 100 per cent, but 90 per cent plus I could say the same things again in response to those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to make it clear why I'm waiting after you finish answering your question, I'm waiting in order for the interpretation to be complete before I start putting my next question to you. And is what is recorded in this statement true, according to your best recollection?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Everything that I said I stand by. I stand by everything that is in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Although you have already partly answered my next question, let me put that question to you again. If I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answer be the same?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: As I've already told you, Mr. Lukic, 99 per cent of that would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender the statement of Mr. Kecman.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D1047, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1047 is admitted. Mr. Kecman, we take a break. We would like to see you back in 20 minutes from now. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at ten minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, when I drew your attention to this title, I think a simple observation that it was a mistake that it was part of the discussion but that the issue didn't end up in the statement would have simplified the matters very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Mr. Ivetic isn't here but I just wanted to assure the Court that we're not changing our position regarding the agreement of the Mladic whereabouts, and nothing in my question inferred otherwise. But just so everyone is comfortable on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I wasn't part of that discussion, but I was told something by Mr. Miletic -- Ivetic, so I don't know whether disagreement encompasses nights between 14 and 15 and 15th and 16, as Mr. Mladic was in Belgrade or not. And I think it's helpful for the Chambers and us to know. Our understanding is that it does; but if it does not, if the position of the Prosecution is that it does not, then we'll have to proceed differently than we planned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think the first and most important thing is that Mr. McCloskey explains to the Defence, not in court, why he considers his line of questioning not to deviate from the agreed position. And if then anything remains, then of course -- then at a later time, we'll hear from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kecman, we'll continue. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would read a statement summary of Mr. Kecman now, and then with your leave, I would have some questions for this witness as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Janko Kecman is a retired air force colonel. Upon completion of the military academy holding the rank of second lieutenant, he went to Zagreb and started working at the Pleso airport with the helicopter squadron for anti-armour combat. The unit was of mixed ethnic composition. He lived in Zagreb in the settlement where almost all the pilots of his squadron lived. He remembers when HDZ members blocked his settlement using trucks loaded with sand. In March 1991, after the conflict at Plitvice, helicopters from his 111th Aviation Brigade were sent to transport their wounded. After this conflict, the siege and blockade of the Pleso airport commenced. His squadron transported customs officers who were to take over the border crossings in Slovenia. After the helicopters with customs officers landed, the Slovenian Territorial Defence immediately captured them and put them in refrigerator trucks. First JNA helicopter was shot down in Slovenia above the place called Ig. Mr. Kecman took part in the transfer of the squadron to Bihac, B&H. On the 13th of December, 1991, Mr. Kecman was shot down for the first time in Mackovac village in Western Slavonia. He was attacked from the tower of a Catholic church. He did not want to shoot at the church although he had information that Croatian forces were attacking from there. He knows that the Muslim-Croat helicopters flew the whole time during the war, 1992 to 1995. They were stationed at the safe area of Bihac and the safe area of Sarajevo. They used helicopters throughout the war to supply their forces in the safe areas, especially those of Bihac and Srebrenica, with combat equipment. In addition to using helicopters, Muslim forces also used AN-26 transportation planes for supply purposes and those planes would land at the Coralici airport. That was statement summary and I would now proceed with the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kecman, what do you know about the illegal arming in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, when did that start, and who was it who engaged in those activities?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: As I've already told you, Mr. Lukic, that started in 1990 and 1991 and then throughout the war until 1995. How can I endorse my statement? When members of other ethnic groups left the ranks of the JNA, most of them took weapons with them. Secondly, a lot of the weapons was stolen from our unit. Thirdly, we are aware of the Spegelj case. The Croatian guards were being armed and the case was widely publicised in the media. And then the supply also went by air, not only by land routes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to stop you there. Mr. Lukic, apparently you are eliciting sweeping statements. Those were armed during the whole of the war. Please ask the witness about what he observed, specific knowledge on matters he saw, he heard, rather than tell us what you know about, and then we get sweeping statements and references to what everyone knows. That's not assisting the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kecman, as I have asked you, what do you personally know about the arming of Muslim and Croatian sides?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, let me tell you very concretely. When the Ugandan plane landed bringing Kikas at Zagreb airport, I was there. I was present when everything that was on that aircraft was being evacuated to Bihac airport. I can tell you how many sorties we had with transport helicopters to evacuate all that. We flew 14 times to carry military equipment, weapons, and everything else that is needed by armed forces. If we follow a chronology, if needed, of course, I can give you the dates, I can give you the years. I'm here, I can tell you all that. Please ask me. I see that I didn't finish my answer. I'm talking about protected areas. I know about helicopter sorties and I know about aircraft sorties, sorties of transport aircrafts that flew in the direction of protected areas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, Witness, you really should slow down. Otherwise the interpreters are unable to tell us. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just raise to express the concern. I see that the witness is mentioning multiple different possible events within the course of a given answer, and I know the questions are broad. But if we could have some coherence to the transcript that we create and at least have a date or some type of context reference so we can proceed logically through some events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, if --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please try to get to facts rather than, again, to what did you see, when did you see it, what's your source of knowledge, what was it exactly, where was it exactly, that's what we need, not: People were armed over five years. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Give us some concrete examples, please. What did you see yourself?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. I'm talking about the month of August 1991. I'm talking about the transport plane known as Kikas Boeing 707. When all these activities started when the Army of Republika Srpska was established --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You want to talk about the month of August 1991. What and where did you see, hear, anything you want to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my testimony may not be within the context of other testimonies. As a pilot, in the course of our day, I could and I indeed did fly thousands of miles --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I want to know on what mile you saw what, rather than to hear that you flew thousands of miles. What happened in August 1991? And apparently you are talking about a transport plane known as Kikas. Now what would you like to tell us? A specific event.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What happened, first of all? Do you remember what date it was in August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't remember the exact date. I can be mistaken by a day. I know that it was in August 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I stop you there. Where were you when you saw or heard anything that is relevant for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was by that plane, by the Kikas plane, at Pleso airport. And I also went to Zeljevo airport where all the equipment was offloaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did you see when you were near that plane which is relevant for us to know or what did you hear? Or what did you observe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the plane was full of weapons, rifles, there was a lot of equipment, not just weapons but also other military equipment could be seen in that plane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. To whom belonged that plane?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was Ugandan, owned by a Ugandan company. It was hired by merchants of arms who smuggled weapons for the Army of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say it was a Ugandan plane which was involved in smuggling weapons. How did you see that there were arms on that plane? Did you go into that plane? Did you saw them unload it? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I entered the plane several times. Not only then but also later when that same aircraft carried thousands of people to Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Judge is asking you about weapons. Forget people. Please answer the Judge's question.

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I saw the weapons because we opened the crates where those weapons were, and my colleagues would take a rifle or two as a souvenir to remind of that contingent of weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I leave it in your hands, but this is the way in which it makes sense to elicit evidence from a witness so as if he says it was a company involved in smuggling, what was that company, how does he know all that, in what capacity was he entering that plane. That's what we would like to hear what he can tell us. Please proceed and keep it strict.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for clarification. Witness, could you please tell us who are the "we" who opened crates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can, Your Honours. The pilots who transported the contingent from the helicopter to Bihac airport. Members of helicopter crews that transported all that, the whole contingent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you could also try to find out where Pleso airport exactly is. Is that -- but, Mr. Lukic, I think I've been clear enough on what would assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kecman, could you please tell us where Pleso airport is.

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: The Pleso airport is about 10 kilometres away from Zagreb, the capital of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what do you know, which company, which person was involved in the smuggling of the weaponry, what do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, somewhere in my papers --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just give us the name, please. We're not going to have enough time to do anything. Just answer the question, please. Who was involved in the smuggling of the weapons?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I cannot remember now what the name of the person is, but I can very easily get that information. You can look on the internet. I mean, I can provide that information for you very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, this Chamber usually does not find its evidence on the internet, although it's not for the full hundred per cent excluded. If you don't know the name, just tell us: I don't know the name. That's sufficient. Do you remember the name of the company that was involved, because you referred to a company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the sign on the plane indicates clearly where it was from. I was next to the plane, I could see that. On the other hand, I could see the content of the cargo there. And the third thing -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm stopping you again. You were talking about a company involved in smuggling. Now, an air carrier is not necessarily in control of what is onboard of a plane. What's the name of the air carrier, what name was found on the plane, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about who had control over the cargo in that plane, who ordered it to be transported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I'm saying - and I hope that I was clear in my previous answers - the weapons were intended for the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, if you continue not to answer questions but, rather, tell us what you consider important, then we have to -- sooner or later, we have to stop you and then we have to establish that you're not answering our questions. My question was: You earlier referred to a company involved in smuggling. Do you know which company was responsible for the cargo in the plane, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We give it another try, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How do you know, Mr. Kecman, that the weapons were intended for the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: How do I know that? You could see from the documents that were in the airplane, and you could see in the papers it was stated who the person or the ordering party was and to whom the contingent should be delivered. And that information was there, it existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And another part of the question put to you by Judge Orie. In what capacity did you enter the plane?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: We waited for the goods to be unloaded from the plane and into the helicopter, so it was our task as the crew to wait and wait until the plane was unloaded. That was not our job. We were supposed to take over and fly the plane so we did not get involved in the unloading part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your question has not been answered, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In what capacity, what was your function, when you were present at that place?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: I was a member of the crew.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who sent you there or were you already there?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: The assignment were -- was received from our superior command. We received the assignment to transport the cargo from Pleso airport to Zeljeve [phoen] airport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're talking about being a member of the crew, a crew of the plane or a crew of the helicopter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Mi8 helicopter crew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I understand that you were expected to wait until the cargo from the plane was loaded into the helicopter and that you would then transport it any further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you earlier told us that the documents in the plane revealed the ordering party and to whom the contingent should be delivered. Who was the ordering party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. We, as pilots, did not have any insight as to who issued the order for the transport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but you said you could see in the papers it was stated who the person or the ordering party was. Now, what's the name of the person or what's the name of the ordering party as you saw it in the documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall the name of the person, but as for the name of the party -- yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please tell us what the name of the party is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name of the party was the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what did the paper say as to whom the contingent should be delivered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, these were bills of lading, so the cargo that was being shipped, it was irrelevant. It had its accompanying documents, and the technician would receive the cargo. The bill of lading would accompany the shipment from the place of loading to the place of unloading. That was not part of our job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said that you could see in the papers to whom the contingent should be delivered. Did you intend to say that is what you can see in these kind of papers or did you intend to say that you saw it in those papers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, how can I explain that to you? We were not there alone. It was not just us, the crew. There was a large number of people around the plane, there were people from security, number one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop you there. What did you see? Did you have a look at those papers or did you not have a look at those papers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not look at the bills of lading, but I looked at the documentation about the plane, which I was interested in because it's my profession, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Next question: How then, as you explained earlier, could you tell us that the cargo was -- that the Croatian government was the ordering party if you didn't have a look at those papers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we're human and so there were a number of people moving around that live organism. My colleagues were there who saw the papers, and we discussed those documents and the bills of lading and the accompanying documentation as well as the cargo itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you didn't see those papers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please proceed. Let's give it another try and let's get to facts rather than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kecman, you mentioned it but it wasn't recorded in the transcript. What kind of guns did you see in that transport?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: There were SRP66 [as interpreted] rifles on the transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that once again slowly. I think it was not recorded properly in the transcript, slowly.

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: The rifles were SAR-56 millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to correct now; it would take too much time. It's 5.56. 56 millimetres cannot be a gun, a hand-held gun, it would be a cannon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I appreciate Mr. Lukic's deduction --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's just assume that's what the witness said, the whole relevance -- but apparently there were weapons and the witness has described them. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kecman, did the JNA have any guns of 5.56 millimetre calibre?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: No, it did not, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And let us concentrate now. Can you please tell us what you personally know about flights into the Bihac protected area in connection with weapons?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, since this is a broad topic --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I was just going to raise just so we have some context when. I have no problem with Mr. Lukic somewhat directing the witness to at least a year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, if you answer the question, could you at least indicate what year you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can. We're going to talk about 1992 from the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska on the 12th of May, 1992, then until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak a little bit farther away from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now you are invited not to come too close to the microphone if you speak. Tell us, Witness, answer the question now that was put to you: What you personally know about flights into the Bihac protected area in connection with weapons? And you'll now focus on 1992 after the 12th of May. And, again, give us facts. You may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in that period, 1992, I was a member of the Army of the Serbian Krajina as commander of the helicopter squadron at the Udbina airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where Udbina is?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: The Udbina airport is located north of the town of Knin, some 70 to 80 kilometres away from that town and in the area of the Plitvice lakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what did you see in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Since we had the option to fly in the area of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina in 1992, the no-fly zone did not apply to the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, but as of the 1st of August, 1992, it applied only to Republika Srpska. So we pilots who flew in the Republic of the Serbian Krajina had the option of carrying out our flights without having to announce them in advance to the SFOR in that area. The area covered the Zemunik airport, included Knin, and to the north through Lika, Banja and Kordun, and Western Slavonia and eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now go back to the question. What did you see regarding the flights that had weapons in the direction of Bihac?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Well, our information is -- and I have to just say something to you. The army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and of Republika Srpska had eyes and ears, and I am saying this because we had radar positions at the most prominent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear the evidence of those eyes and ears. What we're interested in at this moment is your eyes and your ears. Could you tell us what you saw in relation, that's to start with, that is shipping weapons in the direction of Bihac. What did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it was the period from 1992. Now I'm going to tell you specifically. So the first activity when the plane of the B&H army was downed in the area of Bihac, we can say that that specifically happened on the 7th of May, 1994. And then on the 28th, I'm talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. We take it step by step. Apparently you are telling us that there was a plane of the B&H army was downed in the area of Bihac on the 7th of May. What did you see? What did you observe in relation to that? Where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in the area and I can tell you the following: We had intelligence data that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was supplying itself from the Zagreb logistics base --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we'll come to that later. First I'd like to know what did you observe yourself ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I as the commander of the squadron did not only deal with flight matters. I was also involved in other intelligence tasks because I wanted to create conditions for my unit also to fly safely in that area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you first answer my question. What did you observe yourself in relation to that plane of the BH Army which was downed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not talking about this first supposition, I'm not talking about the plane, I'm talking about the Mi17 helicopter in our --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm asking you about the plane. You started your answer by saying the first activity -- when the plane of the BH Army was downed in the area. Do you say you have no personal -- you didn't personally observe anything of that and that you only could tell us about what you did after that? Is that what you intend to tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I want to give you a chronology. I want to give you all of the activities to make it possible for you to understand about the situation on the ground. Under one, I would like to say there was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Witness. I can imagine what your -- the purpose is. What we have on our mind is that we expect you to answer the questions. You were talking about the shipment of weapons, and you started telling us about a plane which was downed on the 7th of May. What we're interested in is what do you know by personal observation about that event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Bear with me. I'm talking about a helicopter. I was standing next to it. It was downed in the area of Slunj flying from Cetina to Zagreb. That plane was downed by our units. It was not a plane, it was a helicopter. I apologise. The minister of foreign affairs, Mr. Ljubijankic, was on that helicopter. Beside that, for months we were engaged in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you are telling what happened. And what I'm interested in is what you observed yourself. But Mr. Weber was on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to put on the record that I'm lost. We've shifted between planes, now helicopters, dates, locations, area of Bihac. So I just want to put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, apparently we moved -- unless this helicopter was on its way to Bihac, but we are in Slunj at this moment, if I understand the witness well. I try hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We all do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I give you another chance to do it. But please, Witness, listen to the question. Answer the question. Apparently there's something about a helicopter, not a plane, which was downed on the 7th of May which you link to transportation of weapons, although you now tell us that someone was on board. Let's take it step by step and just focus on what you know, how you know it, what you did see. Mr. Lukic, I give you another chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kecman, I have to tell you one thing. You don't understand our environment at all. If you don't answer my question, your answer doesn't count at all. If I ask you about Bihac and then you start talking about Tuzla, it doesn't count. If I ask you about sorties of planes carrying weapons into Bihac protected area, I need you to tell me about Bihac. Please focus. I don't know whether it's me or what. What did you tell us about Slunj? What kind of plane? And please make a distinction. I saw this, I heard this as a commander, this was intelligence I received. It doesn't really matter whether you saw things personally or not, but you have to give us the source of your intelligence or information.

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I am talking about the supply of weapons to Bihac incurred using both aircraft and helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Tell us about planes, about aircraft.

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Okay, aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, aircraft.

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Aircraft that were used to supply the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, more specifically Bihac pocket, were aircraft AM 26, property of Ukraine, with Ukrainian crews.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Among those Ukrainians, was there anybody else, and in what capacity, do you know and how do you know it?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. Apart from Ukrainian crews, there were also pilots of BiH army. They were the ones who were crew leaders because they were more familiar with the area, they were more familiar with the circumstances, and they could communicate with the people on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the source of that information? How do you know that crew members were also members or pilots of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina who flew together with Ukrainians?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: This is how it is -- it was, Mr. Lukic: A plane was downed after having air-dropped material in the area of Coralic, north-west of Bihac. It was an auxiliary airport. On the way back, after having air-dropped its cargo, one of the aircraft was hit by our [indiscernible] rocket and that aircraft fell in Plasko area in the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we still do not know how you knew that crew members were also pilots of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina because that was the question. How did you know that apart from the Ukrainian crew there were also pilots of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we carried out an investigation about downing of that aircraft. I was a member of that team. I was at the place where the aircraft had fallen. We found complete documentation pertaining to the aircraft as well as the pilot's documents. The pilot who belonged to the BiH army. We did not find any documents on his body. We collected all those bodies into a body-bag, as it were, and we took them to Knin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Take it step by step again. Apparently you found at the place where the plane was downed, you found bodily remains. You put them in a body-bag. Now, next question is: When and how was that person, which as you told us did not have any documents on himself, how was that person identified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you, Mr. President, this is what it was all about. Knowing that the crews were Ukrainian, we handed the bodies over to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, I stop you -- stop --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me, allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm not allowing you to again and again move away from the question. Who identified the bodies you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bodies were identified in Knin by medical experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what was the method used? Was it by DNA? Was it -- how was it done and is there any report about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what method was used. I'm not a professional of that kind. We were an investigation team, and we reported to the command about what we had found there on the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that person of whom the bodily remains were found, was that person identified by name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. He was a pilot and, if I'm not mistaken, his name was Samir Begic and he was from Cazin. Two years ago, two years ago, his brother turned to me with a request to tell him what had happened to his brother's bodily remains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Lukic, you now take the witness back to the relation between where the arms apparently had been dropped, how it could still be established that the arms were transported by that plane.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kecman, you heard Judge Orie's question and what is important for this case. What is your knowledge? How was it established that the weapons were transported by that plane if the weapons had already been dropped from the plane --

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: And I'm putting another question --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, you cannot be putting questions. All you can do is give answers. So what is your knowledge? Do you have personal knowledge, intelligence, did you read it in the papers? Just tell us your source of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: It was on the basis of intelligence that we had that we knew that the flights were originating from Krk airport towards the Coralici protected area and then from then on to the airport Pleso in Zagreb and the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when you say "intelligence," are you able to be more specific? Was that your intelligence organ or the organ of another unit? How did that work?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I wanted to say earlier that as part of the republic -- of the Serbian Krajina air force, there was a battalion that had a number of radars, and so thanks to those radars we had a complete overview of all the flights. And our units in the field observed that flight, they saw it, and that flight was unannounced. And for that reason, ambushes were set up in those areas. This is one of the usual tactics that is applied in situations like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say "unannounced." Were there any announced flights and how did you react in such situations?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: We're going back to what has already been said. What is this all about? A number of flights - I'm now speaking about the Army of the Republic of the Krajina that we were conducting, we had to announce flights going to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. We also had to announce all flights to Banja Luka. We could not venture past Banja Luka. We would announce those flights one week ahead, and then SFOR forces would monitor those flights upon departure and arrival. So they monitored everything that we were doing. The pilot had to have a checklist of all the passengers and the cargo that he was transporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we're talking about flights of the Army of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. I wanted to ask you about the flights that were announced, the flights of the other side. How did you monitor UNPROFOR flights, for example? Could you tell us who announced which flights to whom?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Again we are going to go back. We had an overview, complete overview, of the situation in the air. We had radar overview. All of our commands, including our commander, had a complete picture in his operations centre, so we could monitor from the operations centre the entire situation in the air-space.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're lay-people so you have to understand that, so we need explanations for those technical things. How did you differentiate between an UNPROFOR flight and an unannounced flight that was carrying weapons, for example?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Let me explain. Each aircraft has its identifier and that shows up on the radar screen on the monitor. The markings are seen so we knew which NATO flights there were. So in the course of four years, we even got to know the crews of the flights. We had so much experience that we knew which pilot was flying in which sector, were they pilots from Aviano [phoen], I mean, we had all this intelligence available. And just by looking at the radar screens, we would get that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No loud speaking, Mr. Mladic. Mr. Witness, you were talking about investigation. Has an investigative report been produced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That report was submitted to the command of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina. Let me just add to this. Since the aircraft had fallen in the area of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it might save us a lot of trouble by looking at such a report rather than -- apart from relevance at this moment, whether it's -- that still escapes, to some extent, our minds, and I'm speaking not only on behalf of myself. Yes. Would Mr. Mladic refrain from communicating with the public gallery. If you would turn to this Bench, Mr. Mladic, then you would have the right focus because it's happening here. Mr. Lukic, again relevance. I do not know, but it might give us facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kecman, what happened to the bodily remains of the pilots that had died in the crash? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the -- those bodily remains were put in a tin casket and then Mr. Sabosa [phoen] would arrange for their transport to Belgrade, where they were handed over to the embassy of Ukraine. Because we had realised that those were citizens of Ukraine. At that moment, we were not aware of the fact that among those bodies, there were also bodily remains of the other pilot whom I mentioned previously, the one from Cazin. And then the embassy of Ukraine did not want to take over the casket. And then Mr. Savo Strbac arranged the burial of those bodily remains in the cemetery in Novi Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it's break time or you want to add something, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But I would have one other question. You said at that time you were not aware of the fact that among those bodies there were also bodily remains of the other pilot. You told us a minute ago that the bodily remains of that pilot had been identified. So it's difficult for us to understand why you were not aware that the bodily remains of that pilot were among those where it had been identified, if I understand you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I told you that we did not find any documents belonging to the Muslim pilot who was on that aircraft. We only found documents belonging to the Ukrainian pilots. Only later when the family approached us did we realise that it was common practice for those flights to include a pilot of the BiH army among crew members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's another sweeping statement, but do I understand that it was only after you had offered the bodily remains to be given to the Ukrainian representative, that only after that the identification of that one Bosnian pilot took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Bosnian pilot was identified when the family addressed the BiH army and all other people of good will to have the bodily remains back so that the family could bury its member with dignity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when was that, that it was identified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it was in 2012. The fallen pilot's brother approached me personally to inquire about the situation on the ground that I had eye-witnessed at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was relatively recently. You may follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes, Mr. Kecman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I leave it, to some extent, in your hands how to proceed, but the witness is apparently unable to suppress his inclination to deal with matters which were not asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was facing the same problem a couple of last days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand that. Nevertheless, you should either elicit useful evidence from this witness or give it up and then we'll have what we have, and Mr. Weber will cross-examine the witness and may face similar problems. How much time do you think you would need? And I earlier already hinted that the relevance is not immediately apparently to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think you can expect that I'm just at the beginning of my questions but I'll try to condense them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Otherwise you have to accept that the witness you called and the witness that was interviewed before, that he acts as he does. I mean, you were the only one who could foresee this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not since couple of days ago, Your Honour. I never saw him before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well -- yes, you didn't see him, but I'm talking about the Defence. That includes your team members that should have warned you perhaps about -- and, again, try to find what really is relevant. A lot may not be relevant. But whatever happens, facts, nothing else. We'll take a break and we'll resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you have an opportunity to try to get some useful evidence from this witness and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you should focus at concluding that at quarter past 2.00, focusing on the most relevant parts first. And if it continues to be the same as it was, then I would not further insist -- again, if this was about one of the core issues of the case, then it might have been different. But it seems, to some extent, at least some of the evidence rather in the margin than the core of the case. Please keep that in mind and try to conclude by quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will need -- oh, but there is no usher. I want to call D1047 so we have it on our screens. I'll go through perhaps -- I'll ask for some clarifications from the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kecman, try to carefully listen to the questions and try to focus your answer exclusively on what is asked. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kecman, we have to finish by 2.15 today; our part of this conversation, I mean. Please look at your statement and find paragraph 7 in it. It's on page 3. In paragraph 7, you mention that your helicopters were sent to transport the wounded after the conflict at Plitvice. What was the ethnicity of those whom you transported?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, that was in March 1991, the conflict at Plitvice. There were a lot of wounded, a lot of dead as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, what ethnicity those you transported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean what ethnicity were the wounded? The wounded were both Croats, Muslims, and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have just told us who the wounded were. Whom did you transport? Did you transport all the three ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Yes, all the three ethnic groups were transported.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Where did you transport them?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: The wounded were transported to the military hospital in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be instructed not to come so close to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. When they arrived at the military hospital in Zagreb, what happened to the wounded?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Let me explain my role first. We used our combat helicopters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. One helicopter landed. There were Croatian guards members in it and that helicopter landed at the military hospital. The next helicopter flew over and went to Kerestinac, and Kerestinac is a prison on the periphery of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question was: What happened to the wounded when they arrived in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very simple. One group of the wounded belonging to the Croatian guards stayed at the military hospital in Zagreb, whereas Serbs from Plitvice were taken to Kerestinac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Judge Moloto is asking about Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Let me just tell you, the MUP of the Republic of Croatia had a special unit whose members were also Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we still --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- don't know what happened to the Muslims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- the wounded Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They stayed together with the Croats in the military hospital in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How come that the Serbs ended up in the prison, that they were wounded and they were not left in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Both transport helicopters landed in front of the hospital and the personnel that received the wounded, they received the wounded Croats like I just told you, whereas the other helicopter was sent in the direction of Kerestinac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 11 in your statement, please. In paragraph 9, you're talking about the National Guard Corps, and then in paragraph 11 you say that there were many Muslims from Bosnia-Herzegovina in [indiscernible] as well as Siptars from Kosovo. How do you know? Can you tell us something about the security provided for the airport, what did you see there?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, my unit, the entire helicopter squadron, was based at Lucko airport which is north-west of the city of Zagreb. We shared the Heliodrom with the MUP, with the helicopter unit of the Croatian MUP. Since our perimeter was the same, we often met each other. We flew together in co-ordinated sorties, and we observed a large number of new men who provided security for that Heliodrom. Secondly, coming to work and going back home, we noticed new police officers who were not there before. They were members of the National Guard Corps. They would stop us every day. They ill-treated us. We asked for things that they never -- that they had never asked for before. All that created a negative impact between the members of the military and the National Guard Corps. The senior members of National Guards Corps, i.e., senior officers, were very fair so we often went to see them to insist on them protecting us. We were wanting to know who these newcomers were and why they were treating us the way they did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us how you knew that they were Siptars, because you've now talked a whole page about all kind of things, but not a clue yet to how did you know that there were many Siptars among them?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Judge, I just raise -- just so there's clarity that -- I mean, I know it's in the statement, but the word "Siptar" being referred to, I know has different views by different maybe ethnicity -- based on the ethnicity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- of the person, it's referring to ethnic Albanian in a certain context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, if the witness wouldn't know what we refer to when we were talking about Siptars, that's another matter. Could you tell us, how did you know there were Siptars among them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the building where I lived was 500 metres away from the Zagreb fairgrounds. Secondly, there was a National Guard Corps unit which had been recruited from all over the place, and there were people in that unit that they needed. Second of all, in my unit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop you there again. Did they tell you, did their colleagues tell you, or was there any other way you found out that they were Siptars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw that. I was among them. I socialised with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine. That's a short answer. We don't need a whole page for that. It was -- Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did a member of your unit transgressed, made a breach of discipline with regard to that unit and men in that unit?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: One of our operatives whose name I can't remember was an Albanian, he was a crew member in our unit. Our security forces found him red-handed in transporting people from Kosovo to Zagreb --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the year when that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the year when this happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now paragraph 15, please, that's on the following page. We can see here that an Mi8 helicopter with a mixed crew was shot down. What happened to the crew when that happened?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Let me tell you what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just tell me what their lot was.

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: The crew were all killed because the helicopter exploded when it was air-borne.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have the rest of that in this paragraph. And now on to paragraph 17, please. You say that MEDEVAC, Mrlak, was shot down; he was a Slovenian. What happened to him, what happened to Mrlak after he was shot down?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Mrlak was a commander in Ljubljana, in Slovenia, and his task was to transport food for the units in the area. A rocket was launched at his helicopter. The helicopter was downed and Mr. Mrlak got killed in the accident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any time-frame for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: That was in the month of June, around the 25th of June, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to ask you something about 1993 and 1994 and the Autonomous Region of Western Bosnia. What happened in 1993, something that had to do with Bihac pocket and the Autonomous Region of Western Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: When we're talking about Bihac pocket, it was an enclave with some 300.000 people living in it. It was fully encircled. On the north, there was Republic of Serbian Krajina, on the south and south-west of the area was Republika Srpska. A conflict broke out in the enclave between members of the Bosnian people or Bosniak people in that area. One group were supporters of Fikret Abdic and the others were members of the 5th Corps led by General Ramiz Drekovic who was then succeeded by General Atif Dudakovic. During that conflict, some of the population, women and children, fled to the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, to the towns of Glina, Petrinja, Vojnic, Virgin Most in the hope that the international community would provide them with an opportunity to cross over Croatia and proceed towards Europe. However, that did not transpire, and the people stayed in the area for a long time. There were some 70- to 80.000 members of Fikret's supporters who had hailed from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say that they stayed longer, how long did they stay? Five days? Ten days? Several months?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Well, I could say it was a number of years. All the buildings that were abandoned at the time, people were looking for shelter, for a roof over their heads. So of all the population, the brunt of it was borne by the people of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. You understand. So taking care of them, providing accommodation, food for them, everything that was necessary for them to survive they had in the area of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, all in the hope that they would go to Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These 70- to 80.000 Muslims, did anybody drive them out of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Nobody drove them out; however, they were trying to find a political solution, what to do with those people, where to accommodate them, because the authorities of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina were -- they were becoming a burden to them in the economic sense. They had to have clothing, accommodation, meals, everything that the people needed to survive that unfortunate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are now going back to the Bihac pocket again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I see at page 80, line 16 the witness says there were some 70- to 80.000 members of Fikret's supporters, and you're referring at page 81, line 3, to 70- to 80.000 Muslims. Is this one and the same thing or are you talking about a different topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Since there was a little break there, I would also add to it, the witness also mentioned the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia and also an area under the 5th Corps. So I don't know if maybe it needs clarifying where these 70- to 80.000 people are at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic will, together with the witness, take care of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kecman, we know it, but for the purpose of the transcript we may need to explain some things a little bit. These 70- to 80.000 people, where did they come from and what ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: These 70- to 80.000 people that I refer to came from the area of the Cazin Krajina. In the Cazin Krajina -- that is actually the Bihac pocket, that is where the Velika Kladusa area was. It's a town in the pocket, so people were leaving that area where the conflict was raging. People were concerned, worried for their lives, and they were moving to the north --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, they came from the area of Cazin Krajina. What was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's exactly the answer to the question. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And were they supporters of Fikret, all of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the name of the area that was established by Fikret Abdic, was that the Bihac pocket, or was that the autonomous --

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: It was a separate area within the Bihac pocket. It was called the Autonomous Region of Western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in the Bihac pocket, were there two components there? Were there Muslims there and Croats and what was their relationship?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Lukic. In one part of it, in the area where the airport was located, that's where the Croatian component was. And the commander in that area was General Santic. It was a smaller group of Croats that were part of the 5th Corps. They waged war together. Mr. Santic and later Budakovic with Republika Srpska Krajina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll stop you again. No one asked you about who was the commander and in what units they were. I do understand from your answer that there were two components: Muslims and Croats. Could you tell us briefly about their relationship.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honour. They co-operated, because they were in the same area, in the encirclement. They worked together in actions against the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just so we don't have confusion, there's reference by this witness to the JNA 5th Corps existing prior --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, well, well, he was not asked about that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, that's why I raised because I see that there's reference on page 82, line 24, to the 5th Corps, and there's two potential 5th Corps that this witness might be referring to, and I believe it's one and not the other. And I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I understand it to be one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's keep it short. Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if you want to rely ever on this reference to the 5th Corps, you should clarify it. If you don't want to rely on it ever --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I thank my learned friend for drawing our attention to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kecman, this 5th Corps that you referred to, is that the 5th Corps of the JNA or the 5th Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: That is the 5th Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's the one that I referred to just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any attempts at negotiations with the opposing side in the Bihac pocket that you are personally aware of? And if yes, who took part in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: I can say that there were negotiations and General Ratko Mladic went to attend one of those negotiations with both sides, the Muslim and the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And do you know what the outcome was of these negotiations? How did the Croatian component behave, what did they want, what was it that they couldn't do?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Based on information from the negotiations from the commanders who took part personally -- but I didn't speak to any of them, we found out that the Croat component wanted to pull out of the conflict. However, they could not separate from the 5th Corps. Why couldn't they separate from the 5th Corps? Simply, in the environs of Bihac there was a Croat population there in Kamenica Kravlje. There were women and children there. And then on the outskirts, on the lines of the front, you had the HVO forces. So even if they had agreed to pull out and not to wage war against the Serbs, then their families would have problems with the 5th Corps of the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you just please tell us how you know that General Mladic attended these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, in that period I was in the area around Bihac, in the helicopters. So in that period, it was not only myself but my colleagues who actually quite often transported General Mladic. And we would meet every day practically with the security personnel. I was ready in Ribic, it's a place close to those Croat lines, so I was there with the helicopter. And we had information there, we had our medical corps there in case anything happened, God forbid, that we could quickly intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever personally transport General Mladic to these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: No, not to the negotiations, but I explained a little bit earlier what my role and function was in those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Did you have information and, if you did, could you please tell us the source of the information regarding the transport of weaponry to Bihac by road. Who took part in that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: It's an interesting question and it boils down to this. As the war progressed during those years, the Bihac pocket was encircled so it would be logical that in the Bihac [indiscernible] there would be dwindling amounts of food and weaponry. Unfortunately, it was quite the opposite. By receiving weapons and food in different ways, I explained earlier that it came by plane and helicopter, a part of it also came over by land. Unfortunately, UNPROFOR units also had an dishonourable role in all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry I'm raising late, but it was a compound question. I believe the witness actually didn't answer part of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Parts of it he did --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: But -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but not all of it. And we'll leave it to Mr. Lukic whether he wants answers to the remainder part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kecman, as my colleague Mr. Weber said, I asked you what your sources of information were, if you can remember that today?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: The source of information -- I cannot give you a specific source by first and last name now, but let me say that I am a pilot who transported both the civilian and the military leadership. The people who were controlling that area, so they monitored the SFOR, and at check-points they would find weapons with SFOR that was not part of their regular equipment and kit. And so that share of the weapons we knew who that was intended for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this is what you learned from persons you transported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I learned that in contacts with people in the field. I was present on a daily basis at one of the commands that was in charge of a specific sector along the lines of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that it was known who the weapons were intended for. We don't know until you tell us.

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Lukic. The weaponry was intended for the 5th Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just briefly like to talk about 1995 now. In the autumn of 1995, what information did you have about the participation of UNPROFOR, NATO, the Croatian army in the fighting in Bosnia and Herzegovina during the time when the western municipalities of Republika Srpska were falling?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: This is a broad question. It's hard to answer it briefly, but I will try. What is it about then? I was born in the Visoka Krajina, the high Krajina, in the location of Bosanski Petrovac. So in late 1995, our forward line of defence was located around Grahovo, and then in those actions in the co-operation between the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the regular Croat army forces, this is the Split agreement if I'm not mistaken, there was a co-ordinated action against the Army of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina and the Army of Republika Srpska. Active assistance to those forces was provided by the forces for rapid reaction, and this can be reinforced by the following. All the defence lines, the anti-aircraft defence that NATO broke, they demolished our communications system, and then only after the NATO actions did the actions of the Muslim and Croat components begin their actions on the 6th of May and the 6th of August against the Serb forces during all the phases before the cease-fire was signed sometime on the 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure about the last date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, these kind of questions are eliciting these kind of sweeping statements. I leave it to you but you are aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kecman, what were you personally in a position to see of that operation? What did you observe regarding the NATO actions?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I personally saw and I personally felt on my own helicopter the actions of the Rapid Reaction Force. I saw the artillery location of the Rapid Reaction Forces. It was located south of Kljuc in the village of Jarice [phoen] and south of Ribnik where the village of Macan [phoen] was. I saw their artillery firing in that period. I also saw an UNPROFOR helicopter, CH-47, that was transporting guns to a hill, elevation 1.550, because that cannon fired us and we didn't know where it could have been acting from. We didn't think that it could have been acting from the hill. Only when we saw the helicopter we realised what this was about. This same helicopter, the CH-49, pulled out a downed Croat helicopter from that hill. That is what I saw myself and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just seek clarification. You said you saw an UNPROFOR helicopter CH-47 that was transporting guns. Did you see those guns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could see from a distance that it was transporting a gun. You could see the cargo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The cargo was not inside the helicopter or was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The gun was being transported by being suspended outside of the helicopter, so it was not inside the helicopter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We just have a minute, Mr. Kecman, so I just wanted to ask you: Pilotless aircraft, did you see any?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Well, this is an interesting question. In Drvar, when we were there, these drones were Croat. I personally tried to down that drone by taking off and trying to attain a certain altitude so that I could take it out with a machine-gun. However, since it's a small target, it was white, at an altitude, that was impossible for me because I did not have a guiding mechanism on the ground that would enable me to hit that device --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness repeat their last two questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Last two questions and answers, could they be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kecman, my question was not recorded; neither was your answer. Were there any UNPROFOR drones around?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Yes, there were, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us where you saw them?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: I saw them in the sector of Sanski Most in the village of Kamicuk [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what were they doing there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before we -- when did you see them in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Time-wise it was on the 8th of October, 1995. The time was approximately 1430 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell us what was the role of those drones?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: Those drones were supposed to transfer or report on the actual data in the field. By recordings from the air, they knew the complete deployment of our forces on the ground, and they transferred that information to their command centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time who was attacking the Army of Republika Srpska there?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: During that period, the forces of the 5th Corps, the forces -- the regular Croatian army forces, and what I mentioned here, the Rapid Reaction Force were all attacking Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to -- you to repeat when you said time-wise it was on the 8th of, and then you mentioned the month, in 1995 at approximately 1430 hours. What month did you mention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was October 1995. I was talking about the specific actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They do have all the other information. It was just the month. And just something that has to do with paragraphs 40 to 42. Do you know - and how did you find out if you do know - how many flights were carried out by helicopters that belonged to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the war?

utterances.speaker: JANKO KECMAN
utterances.text: I did find that piece of information. However, that information is something that each side now boasts as to how many flights they carried out. I found out the information regarding the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina regarding the helicopters that they had, the Muslims had six helicopters and we had eight and the Croatian side had four. The Bosnian army helicopters carried out over 7.000 flights. They transported about 30.000 fighters. They transported 3.000 wounded persons. They transported more than 300 tonnes of lethal and other devices. This is information that I came across in the publication of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina where they provide their information about what they did during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not that much interested in what you read elsewhere. Mr. Lukic, if it's really relevant then I take it that you could produce those reports which would then give that information. Mr. Lukic, I have to urge that you conclude now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, then I will conclude now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kecman. This is all we had for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is supposed not to speak aloud. We'll conclude for the day. Mr. Kecman, we'd like to see you back on Monday because we're not sitting on Friday, 9.30 in the morning. But I'd first -- I want to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given. If that's clear to you, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I just wanted to inform the Defence and the Chamber just for the purposes of Monday that I do probably expect to be under a session with the witness, just for witness scheduling purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There was one other matter, and since we are at the end of the week, unfortunately I have to perhaps pay attention to it. Very briefly. Mr. Lukic, you told us this morning that two witnesses initially scheduled for the week of the 18th to the 22nd of May would not come to testify. Were you referring to Mr. Milijanovic and Mr. Tomasevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me consult, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we will have four witnesses for that week, and this morning with the -- in conversation with my learned friend Weber, we estimated that we would be fine for that week for five working days with those four witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let me just have a look. Yes, so we have then -- you said four witnesses or five?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that would then be -- I think there are no protective measures for any of those witnesses, that would be Sokanovic, Pajic, and then we have pending the Chamber's decision on addition to the -- your 65 ter list, perhaps Mr. Savo Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the fourth one would be ... ?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Misic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Misic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Milutin Misic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And it's our understanding that the last one mentioned would actually be the third one that week with the added one being the final --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But we now know the four names of the witnesses who you expect will appear to testify. Apologies for our late -- for the late conclusion of today. We'll adjourn for the day and we'll resume Monday, the -- that will be the 11th if I'm not mistaken -- the 11th of May, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 11th day of May, 2015, at 9.30 a.m.
